content.content:
1	# Task 11: Crate pyramid and wrecking ball
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. Show an outdoor concrete yard containing a stack of wooden crates arranged as a pyramid of 5 rows (5,4,3,2,1 crates, 15 in total, each crate a 1 x 1 x 1 cube). The stack must stand stably under gravity without collapsing on its own. Beside the stack, a heavy steel wrecking ball hangs from a tall crane arm on a rigid chain or rope (a pendulum with a fixed pivot and fixed length of about 6 units). The user presses an on-screen button 'Swing' to pull the ball back to a starting angle of 60 degrees and release it; it then swings down and smashes into the pyramid, scattering crates under rigid-body physics (gravity, collisions, friction, restitution). A 'Reset' button rebuilds the stack and returns the ball to rest. Use a fixed physics timestep. Add a soft key light with shadows, a subtle sky or background, and a camera that frames both the crane and the stack. Expose a read-only window.__TASK_STATE__ = { phase: 'ready'|'swinging'|'settled', crates: number, displaced: number, ballAngleDeg: number } updated every frame, where displaced counts crates whose centre has moved more than 0.75 units from its initial position. No external network assets.
4	
5	## Rendering contract (all tasks)
6	
7	- Draw into the existing `<canvas id="app">` (640x360 CSS pixels, device pixel ratio 1). Do not resize it or create another canvas.

content.thinking:
It resolves, so the compat package exists, but it's not declared in package.json even though it's present in node_modules. That's a bit risky since relying on an undeclared dependency feels fragile for grading, so maybe it's safer to just implement the physics myself instead of depending on it.

Given the ambiguity around whether that package is sanctioned, I decide to go conservative and build my own physics: OBB boxes plus sphere collisions, sequential impulses with SAT-based box-box contact manifold clipping, aiming for a stable pyramid of boxes. It's more work than using Rapier but avoids any dependency risk, so I start by removing the probe code and overwriting it.

Now I'm designing the physics bodies: boxes with half-extent 0.5, a dynamic sphere ball with higher mass connected to a pivot via a distance constraint (treated as a rigid rope), and a static ground plane. I decide to give the ball infinite rotational inertia to simplify things, skipping rotation and friction complexity for it while still handling ball-crate collisions normally.

I'm figuring out the crane pendulum geometry — placing the pivot so the ball rests just beside the crate pyramid, calculating the swing arc from a 60° starting angle, and working out pivot height and ball radius so it sits properly above the ground at rest before being released to strike the stack.

At this angle the ball center sits around y≈1.12, so it clips the bottom row and a bit of the second row, which lines up with the offset pyramid structure where each row is centered and half-offset from the one below for stability. I'm considering nudging the pivot height slightly so the resting ball position lands a bit cleaner against the stack.

I want the pivot at roughly y=6.85 so the ball, with radius 0.8, hangs just barely clear of the ground, and since the ball moves along a fixed arc it should never physically dip below that even during the swing, though I'll also add a sphere-plane check for safety. I'm also working out the phase logic: starting in 'ready', moving to 'swinging' once released, then transitioning to 'settled' once the crates have been slow or asleep for a sustained period after impact.

Since the pendulum keeps oscillating with damping for a long time, I realize settling should really be judged by the crates' state rather than the ball's, so I'll add air drag to the ball and define 'settled' as crates staying below a speed threshold for about a second post-impact, with a time cap as backup. I'm estimating the period of the swing (around 4.9s) and that the ball should reach the bottom and hit the crates at roughly 1.7 seconds in, which I'll use to gate when the settling check can start.

For reporting the ball's angle, I want a signed value where pulling back reads as positive, so I'm computing it from the ball's position relative to the pivot with the sign set so pulled-back equals +60 degrees, matching the described starting pose. For the swing action itself, I'm deciding to just teleport the ball directly to 60 degrees and release it on press rather than animating the pull-back, since the spec just needs it to start swinging from that angle.

For the physics engine, I'm settling on fixed-timestep integration at 1/120s with a fairly high iteration count (around 30) to keep a 15-box pyramid stable without needing warm-started contact caching, which would add complexity. I'm also planning to add per-body sleeping for stacks that stay below a velocity threshold for half a second, to lock in stability once things settle.

Since collision detection still runs on sleeping bodies, a swinging ball colliding with a resting crate pulls that crate's island awake, since the ball stays part of the connected island as soon as contact forms.

Settling is defined as all crates asleep (and hit), using thresholds like linear speed under 0.08 and angular under 0.1 sustained for 0.6s. For the initial stack, I'm leaning toward starting crates asleep by construction so stability is guaranteed from the outset, rather than risking jitter as they settle naturally under gravity.

Now I'm working out collision detection, starting with box-vs-ground-plane checks by testing each of the box's 8 vertices for y<0 to generate contact points with upward normals, while deciding whether the ground should be an infinite plane with just a finite visual slab so crates don't fall off an edge.

For box-vs-box, I need SAT across the 15 axes (face normals plus cross products of edges), biasing toward face axes for stability, then building a contact manifold by picking the reference face and clipping the incident box's face polygon against the reference face's side planes to generate contact points.

For sphere-vs-box, I'll find the closest point on the OBB to the sphere center and push outward along the nearest face axis if the center is inside the box, and for ball-vs-ground it's just a sphere-plane test. Overall I'll use sequential impulses for the solver, resolving contacts body by body.

I'm deciding to skip warm-starting for simplicity and instead rely on 20-30 solver iterations at 1/120 timestep, accepting that a 5-row stack might show slight sinking or jitter before objects sleep. I'm weighing whether that jitter could interfere with sleeping thresholds, but think the small slop and low Baumgarte beta keep it manageable.

If I do want warm-starting, I'd match contacts across frames per body pair by comparing world-space contact points within a small distance threshold and copying over impulses, keyed by a simple pair index. Then for the integration step, I'd apply gravity to velocities, run the solver, and integrate positions and orientations, computing world inertia tensors from the local inverse inertia transformed by rotation, using three.js vector and matrix types for the math despite the allocation overhead.

Given the scale—15 bodies, roughly 100 contacts over many iterations and steps per second—I want to minimize allocations in the solver's inner loop, reusing Vector3 objects rather than creating new ones, and capping substeps per frame at four. I'm structuring this in a dedicated physics module with its own lightweight vector math built on three.js primitives, starting with a Body class holding position, orientation, velocity, angular velocity, inverse mass, local and world inverse inertia, shape dimensions, and sleep state.

For masses I'm picking a practical ratio—crates at 1, the pendulum ball heavier at 25—so sequential impulses converge without instability through a chain of boxes. The ball's pivot constraint is a distance joint: I compute the vector from pivot to ball center, derive the current length and direction, and solve a velocity-level impulse along that direction using a Baumgarte-style bias term to correct drift, then also hard-project the ball's position back onto the correct radius after integration to kill residual error.

I'm weighing whether to only correct position/velocity after the solve versus treating the rope as a real constraint row inside the iteration loop alongside contacts—since contacts computed against a "free" ball would overestimate radial impulse otherwise. Since most impacts near the bottom are tangential to the rope, the error is small, but I'll do both: include the joint as a bilateral velocity constraint each iteration, plus a final positional projection for safety. For visuals, I'm picturing a simple gray cylinder as the rope connecting the arm tip to the ball rather than a multi-link chain.

Damping settings seem fine: light linear/angular damping for crates, tiny air drag for the ball since it rotates freely with no meaningful inertia. Now I'm working out the box-box collision routine, using separating-axis tests across each body's face normals and their cross-product edge axes to find the minimum overlap, picking the best axis and sign so the contact normal points consistently from body A to body B.

I'm biasing the selection toward face axes over edge axes unless the edge overlap is meaningfully smaller, since parallel stacked boxes produce degenerate edge cross-products that should be skipped. Now I'm setting up the reference/incident face logic for clipping, where the reference face owner determines the outward normal direction and its box center is offset along that normal to locate the contact plane.

Still writing clipping logic...

I'll place the contact point at the midpoint between the point and its projection along the normal, then if there are more than four contact points, I need a way to trim down to the four most significant ones, prioritizing the deepest and most spread-out points.

For the edge-edge collision case, I'm working out the contact normal from the cross product of the two edge axes, then finding the support point on each body's surface along that normal direction.

Next I need to solve for the closest points between the two edge lines using the standard line-line closest point formulas, then take the midpoint as the contact point and compute the depth from the overlap.

For sphere-box collisions, I'm working out the logic: transform the sphere center into the box's local space, clamp it to the box half-extents to find the closest point, and handle both cases where the center is inside the box (using the face with minimum penetration) and outside (computing the normal from the difference vector and comparing distance to radius).

For consistency, I'll always treat the box as body A and the sphere as body B, flipping the normal when needed. For ground contacts, I'm modeling the plane as a static body with zero inverse mass, letting narrowphase handle it generically — for box-vs-plane, I check each of the eight vertices for penetration below y=0, and for sphere-vs-plane I use the simpler depth calculation based on the sphere's radius and center height.

For broadphase, with around 16 bodies giving roughly 120 pairs, a bounding-sphere check is cheap enough to just run on everyone. I'm deciding to generate contacts for every pair each step regardless of sleep state, since islands need full connectivity data to know when a sleeping group should wake up — I'll use union-find across dynamic bodies to build islands, and only skip solving (not contact generation) for islands where every body is asleep.

One concern: resting contacts could oscillate between touching and not touching if I only generate them at exact zero penetration, so I need a slop value (around 0.005) and keep contacts within a small negative-depth margin to avoid jitter from gravity pulling bodies back into slight overlap each frame.

For positive depth beyond slop, I'll push out proportionally with a beta correction factor, clamped to a max push speed, otherwise target zero separating velocity. I'm computing the impulse from the gap between target and actual relative velocity scaled by effective mass, clamping accumulated impulse non-negative, and adding restitution when incoming velocity is fast enough and objects aren't already overlapping.

I'm sketching the contact data structure holding bodies, point, normal, depth, tangents, accumulated impulses, and effective masses, and defining friction clamped per-axis to the normal impulse scaled by friction coefficient, solved before the normal impulse each iteration.

Still writing inertia math...

For the box shape, mass 1 side cube gives simple diagonal inertia values, so I'm using that as a sanity check. Now I'm outlining the per-timestep solver loop: update body axes and inertia tensors, then run collision detection.

Next comes merging bodies into islands via union-find on contacts, where if any body in an island is awake, the whole island wakes up—this keeps sleeping stacks correctly dormant until something touching them stirs. After that, awake bodies get velocity integration from gravity and damping, followed by preparing contacts just for the awake islands to save work on sleeping ones.

Then warm starting applies to those contacts, positions get integrated, and the ball has its constraint projection. Sleep timers accumulate per-body when velocities drop below threshold, with islands sleeping only once every body's timer exceeds half a second—though the ball never sleeps and blocks any island it's part of from sleeping too, and I'm weighing whether the velocity thresholds (0.1 linear, 0.15 angular) might cause a slowly-tipping box to fall asleep prematurely at its apex.

For the warm-start cache itself, I'm storing each contact's normal and friction impulses keyed by contact pair, with friction stored as a world-space vector that gets reprojected onto new tangent directions when matched to a fresh contact point within a small position tolerance. For pairs that get skipped because their island is asleep, I keep their old cached impulses rather than clearing them, so only actively solved pairs get fresh cache entries while sleeping ones retain their previous warm-start values.

For the tangent basis, I'm picking t1 based on whichever axis is least aligned with the normal, then deriving t2 as the cross product of normal and t1, normalizing both. Orientation integration uses a quaternion derivative from angular velocity, pre-multiplied into the current orientation and renormalized each step, with angular velocity clamped to 30 rad/s and gyroscopic effects ignored for simplicity. Now I'm moving on to setting up the three.js renderer for the scene.
